headings.text: 🌳 Decide: how to feed the voice
🔬 To explore: is Cartesia better than Deepgram for our voice?
🏷️ Landscape (as of Oct 2026, LiveKit Inference TTS)

notes.html:
How text becomes the agent's voice fast enough: stream it, cut it into short segments, say the domain terms right, choose a voice that suits the persona, and know when a speech-to-speech model would replace the whole stage.

Where this sits

capture → carry → clean → detect → transcribe → endpoint → think → speak → yield → observe

Reading order

# Note Tier Stage You'll understand
1 Streaming TTS CORE speak TTFB, one stream per segment, warm connections, backup voice
2 Sentence chunking SUPPORTING speak the 12-word flush and what it saved
3 Pronunciation SUPPORTING speak a reviewed lexicon and the round-trip test
4 Choosing a voice SUPPORTING speak gates first, ear second
5 Realtime speech-to-speech SUPPORTING speak when the cascade loses, and the half-cascade
– Background audio BREADTH speak ambience and thinking sounds

Owners

Concept Home
TTFB, streams, warm sockets, the backup voice streaming TTS
Segment rules, the forced flush chunking
Lexicon, respellings, round trip pronunciation
Voice choice, pace, gates vs ear choosing a voice
Realtime and half-cascade specifics realtime models
Cascaded vs realtime as a design choice pipeline shapes
What the voice should sound like as a character persona and personality
What happens when the voice vendor fails degradation ladder

Decide: how to feed the voice

Ask in order If yes → Because
1. Must the exact words be spoken? cascade or half-cascade with your own TTS realtime models don't guarantee scripts
2. Is first-audio time the gate? one stream per segment, sentence end or N-word flush bounds the first segment
3. Does tone break across segments? try one stream per reply (e.g. Deepgram Flux) and measure the TTFB cost prosody vs latency
4. Do domain terms appear? a reviewed lexicon + round-trip test voices guess differently and change

🔊 Our system in one table

Stage What we run Status Measured
speak Deepgram Aura-2 Athena, one stream per segment TTFB p50 342 ms in calls; warm p50 314 ms in goldens (gate 300 ms fails)
speak sentence end or 12-word flush 677 → 437 ms first audio on a long sentence
speak 23-entry lexicon lex-2026-09-24.2 round trip 7/8 on Athena
speak backup OpenAI gpt-4o-mini-tts after 1 retry –
speak no realtime model, no background audio –

To explore: is Cartesia better than Deepgram for our voice?

Short answer, as of 16 Oct 2026: unknown for us; worth one golden run. Cartesia is best known for low-latency TTS (Sonic). Published latency figures are vendor or vendor-adjacent, measured near their servers, and no independent head-to-head of Sonic 3 vs Aura-2 turned up.

Deepgram Aura-2 (what we run) Cartesia Sonic (LiveKit, 16 Oct 2026)
Current models Aura-2 voices; Flux for per-reply reading sonic-3, sonic-3.5, sonic-3.6 (+ dated pins, sonic-latest)
Retiring Inference deepgram/aura (v1) retired 13 Feb 2026 sonic-2, sonic-turbo, sonic-3-2025-10-27 retire 20 Oct 2026 → use sonic-3.5
Pronunciation text respelling (our lexicon) inline IPA overrides, pronunciation dictionaries (Sonic 3)
Speed and emotion voice choice speed 0.6–1.5× (Sonic 3), volume, emotion controls (beta), expressive mode via LiveKit
Timestamps – word, phoneme and normalised timestamps
Languages English voices 42 language codes on Sonic 3; Sonic 3.6 adds Oriya and Urdu
Our measurement warm TTFB 314 ms from India not measured
Published claims Aura-2 under 200 ms TTFB (third-party page) sub-90 ms; Sonic Turbo ~40 ms (roundups)

Why it's worth testing: the 300 ms first-audio gate fails on every Deepgram voice tried, and Cartesia's IPA dictionaries and speed control would address the kubectl miss and Vesta's pace.

How to test:add cartesia/sonic-3.5 to voice/engine.py as a family behind TTS_MODELrun the TTS goldens (lexicon round trip with the lexicon, warm and cold TTFB from India)scripts.voice_ab on the same lines for the earcompare price per character at our volume.

Sources: LiveKit — Cartesia TTS · LiveKit — TTS models · Fish Audio — Cartesia vs Deepgram (vendor) · fast.io — best AI TTS tools 2026.

Open Indic TTS: IISc's DhVaani-0.5 (27 Indian languages, zero-shot) for future non-English voices; see Indic speech at IISc.

notes.title: Streaming Text-to-Speech — Time to First Byte
notes.html:
References

LiveKit — TTS models (read 16 Oct 2026) · ~/Projects/tech_documentation/interview_prep/02-tts.md · ~/Projects/tech_documentation/ADR/voice_pipeline/voice_quality_goldens.md §3–4 · ~/Projects/convo_agentic/meghdootam/voice/engine.py, synth.py

TL;DR

A streaming voice takes text in pieces over an open connection and sends audio back in chunks, so playback starts after the first piece is synthesised, not the whole reply. The number that matters is time to first byte (TTFB): from the moment the first text exists to the first audio frame. Keep the connection warm, feed it the first sentence early, and have a backup voice.

Stage: capture → carry → clean → detect → transcribe → endpoint → think → speak → yield → observe · per turn

Flow: first sentenceTTSSFUheardlater sentences synthesise while it plays

Recall

Prompt Answer
TTFB measures first text available → first audio frame
Why one stream per segment? segment 2 synthesises while segment 1 plays; pooled sockets make streams cheap
What a cold connection costs the TLS + WebSocket setup, hundreds of ms on the first turn
Inside a TTS (classic) text normalisation → phonemes → acoustic model → vocoder; modern models predict audio tokens directly
What if the voice vendor fails mid-call? retry once, then a backup voice, logged
Draw two segments of a reply on a timeline text 1 → synth 1 → play 1; text 2 → synth 2 overlapping play 1 → play 2

The idea

Without it: a 40-word reply is ~1.5 s of synthesis before the first sound (design §8.2).

It does: pipelines synthesis with playback; the person hears the first sentence while the rest is still being made.

It costs: each segment starts a fresh synthesis, so tone can reset between segments; and the first byte depends on network distance to the vendor.

How it works

Rule Because
Warm the connection before the first reply the cold connect is paid on the turn people judge most
Start each segment's stream as soon as its text exists synthesis overlaps playback
Drain every stream to the end abandoning one discards its pooled connection; every later turn then pays a cold connect (a harness bug that read ~1.3 s)
Fall back to a second voice no dead air when the vendor fails

LiveKit API (Oct 2026): tts.stream(), push_text, end_input(), consume SynthesizedAudio; a custom voice path goes in the agent's TTS node. LiveKit deprecates multiple segments per SynthesizeStream, so one stream per segment is the pattern (synth.py).

Knobs

Knob Default Raise it → Lower it →
Feed per segment per reply: one tone through the reply, first audio later –
Retries before the backup voice 1 survives blips, longer silence on failure faster switch
Region of the TTS endpoint vendor's – closer: lower TTFB

🔊 In our system

What Value Status Why / source
Voice Deepgram Aura-2 aura-2-athena-en since 14 Oct 2026 (Flux flux-sienna-en before) engine.py
Feed one stream per segment, started immediately synth.py; Flux per reply was ~115 ms later (454 vs 339 ms)
TTFB in calls p50 342 ms, p95 379 ms as_built §3, 30 days to 16 Oct 2026, India
TTFB gate warm p50 ≤ 300 ms: fails on every voice tried (Athena 314 ms, Sienna 328–339 ms) goldens, 14 Oct 2026; gate not loosened
Cold connect ~620–700 ms, first turn only goldens §3
Backup OpenAI gpt-4o-mini-tts, after 1 retry, switch logged main.py FallbackAdapter

Deviation: the design planned Smallest.ai through a custom adapter; it was never built.

Measure it

  • Metric — tts_node_ttfb p50 and p95 per turn; cold-connect time on the first turn; backup-voice switches.
  • See it — the goldens' TTS-only TTFB (tokens streamed like a model, warm connection).
  • Bounded by — the fallback voice; sentence chunking caps the first segment's length.

Pitfalls

Comparing vendors by their published TTFB

  • Why it's tempting: vendors publish tens of milliseconds.
  • Why it's wrong: those are measured near their servers; ours from India is 314–342 ms including the network.
  • Think instead: measure warm TTFB from your agent's region on your own text.

Measuring with abandoned streams

  • Why it's tempting: a benchmark only needs the first byte.
  • Why it's wrong: dropping the stream discards the pooled connection, so every later sample is a cold connect.
  • Think instead: drain each stream; report warm and cold separately.

Connections

… → think → speak → yield → … — the voice's share of the turn.

  • fed by sentence chunking; stopped by barge-in.
  • says terms right via pronunciation.
  • a line in the latency budget.
  • Say it: Q9 · Q38

notes.title: Sentence Chunking and Flushing — Bounding the First Segment
notes.html:
References

~/Projects/tech_documentation/ADR/voice_pipeline/voice_pipeline_design.md §8.2 · ~/Projects/tech_documentation/ADR/voice_pipeline/voice_quality_goldens.md §4 · ~/Projects/convo_agentic/meghdootam/voice/chunker.py

TL;DR

Cut the reply's streamed text into segments at sentence ends, and force a cut every N words so a long unpunctuated sentence can't hold back the first audio. Shorter first segments mean earlier sound; too short and the voice sounds choppy.

Stage: capture → carry → clean → detect → transcribe → endpoint → think → speak → yield → observe · per turn

Flow: model tokenssentence end, or 12 words?cutlexicon on the segmentTTS stream

Recall

Prompt Answer
Two cut rules sentence-final punctuation, or a forced flush after N words
Our N 12 words
What the flush saved 32-word unpunctuated sentence: first audio 677 → 437 ms
The cost each segment starts a fresh synthesis: tone can "punch" at the start
Draw a 32-word sentence cut at 12 and 24 words three segments; first audio after segment 1

The idea

Without it: the first segment is whatever the model writes before its first full stop; one long sentence and the first byte waits for all of it.

It does: bounds the first segment's length, so the first byte is bounded too.

It costs: prosody across segment boundaries, which a per-reply voice would carry.

How it works

Cut at Pros Cons
sentence end only natural prosody unbounded first segment
sentence end or N words (ours) bounded first byte possible onset "punch" per segment
one stream per reply one tone through the reply first audio later (Flux: 454 vs 339 ms)

The lexicon is applied per released segment, on spoken text only.

Knobs

Knob Our value Raise it → Lower it →
Forced flush (MAX_WORDS) 12 smoother, later first byte earlier first byte, choppier
Cut on sentence end on – –

🔊 In our system

What Value Status Why / source
Rule sentence end or 12 words chunker.py, design §8.2
Effect 677 → 437 ms first audio on a 32-word unpunctuated sentence goldens §4, 24 Sep 2026
Open finding the "punch" may come from cold segment starts, not the voice; sentence-only cuts sampled, not adopted goldens, voice change 14 Oct 2026

Measure it

  • Metric — first-audio time on long unpunctuated replies; listener ratings at segment joins.
  • See it — the goldens' pipelined vs single-stream row.
  • Bounded by — the word cap.

Pitfalls

Cutting on commas to go faster

  • Why it's tempting: more cuts, earlier audio.
  • Why it's wrong: every cut is a fresh synthesis; a comma-cut reply sounds read off cards.
  • Think instead: sentence ends plus a word cap, tuned by ear.

Connections

… → think → speak → … — how text reaches the voice.

  • feeds streaming TTS.
  • applies the lexicon per segment.
  • Say it: Q9

notes.title: Pronunciation — Saying Domain Terms Right
notes.html:
References

~/Projects/tech_documentation/ADR/voice_pipeline/voice_pipeline_design.md §8.3 · ~/Projects/tech_documentation/ADR/voice_pipeline/voice_quality_goldens.md §3–4 · ~/Projects/convo_agentic/meghdootam/voice/vocab.py · LiveKit — Cartesia TTS

TL;DR

A voice that says "en-jinks" for nginx or "jot" for JWT sounds unserious. Keep a small, reviewed, versioned lexicon that respells terms for the voice, apply it only to the spoken text (never the transcript), and test it by synthesising each entry and transcribing it back.

Stage: capture → carry → clean → detect → transcribe → endpoint → think → speak → yield → observe · per session

Flow: segment text ─lexicon: etcd → "E T C D"TTSround-trip check: transcribe it, was "etcd" heard?

Recall

Prompt Answer
Where the lexicon is applied spoken text only; the transcript keeps the spelling
Why reviewed by a person a wrong entry is worse than the voice's default guess
The round-trip test synthesise the respelling, transcribe with a plain listener, check the term
Our gate ≥ 85%
Vendor-native options e.g. Cartesia: inline IPA or pronunciation dictionaries (Sonic 3)
Draw the round trip for one term term → respelling → audio → STT → compare

The idea

Without it: every voice guesses differently, and voices change: Aura's audio for "Kubernetes" was heard as "Coumadetti's" on 12 Oct 2026, though the same listener heard the 24 Sep audio correctly.

It does: pins how each important term is said, versioned per session.

It costs: a list someone maintains, and a test that must re-run whenever the voice changes.

How it works

Entry Respelling Why
etcd "E T C D" "et C D" was heard as "that CD" (24 Sep 2026)
kubectl "cube control" heard back as "KubeControl" on Aura voices: counted as a miss
nginx, k8s, JWT per lexicon defaults are wrong or inconsistent

Knobs

Knob Our value Trade
Lexicon size 23 entries, lex-2026-09-24.2 coverage vs review effort
Mechanism respelling in text portable across vendors; IPA or vendor dictionaries are more precise but vendor-specific

🔊 In our system

What Value Status Why / source
Lexicon 23 entries, pinned per session vocab.py
Round trip, 24 Sep 2026 100% after the etcd fix goldens §4
Round trip, 12–14 Oct 2026 Aura (Andromeda) 75% fail · Flux Sienna 8/8 · Aura Athena 7/8 · Vesta 7/8 goldens §4 and voice change
Target Rubric Compiler proposes terms per role, a person reviews design §8.3

Measure it

  • Metric — lexicon round-trip pass rate per voice, re-run on every voice or model change.
  • See it — goldens/stt_tts TTS section.
  • Bounded by — the version pin: a bad entry is rolled back by version.

Pitfalls

Assuming a voice says a term the same way forever

  • Why it's tempting: it passed once.
  • Why it's wrong: vendor audio changes between syntheses and releases; Aura dropped from 100% to 75% on the same text.
  • Think instead: re-run the round trip on every voice change and on a schedule.

Connections

… → speak → … — the output mirror of keyterms.

  • mirrors keyterm prompting on input.
  • applied per segment by chunking.
  • Say it: Q36

notes.title: Choosing a Voice — By Ear and by Goldens
notes.html:
References

~/Projects/tech_documentation/ADR/voice_pipeline/voice_quality_goldens.md Voice change, 2026-10-14 · ~/Projects/tech_documentation/ADR/voice_pipeline/voice_pipeline_design.md §8.4 · LiveKit — TTS models

TL;DR

Choose a voice in two passes: gates (first-audio time, pronunciation round trip) remove the voices that can't do the job; then listening picks the one that suits the persona. Fix the voice for a whole session, log it, and keep a backup.

Stage: capture → carry → clean → detect → transcribe → endpoint → think → speak → yield → observe · design time

Flow: candidate voicesshortlistchoicefixed per session, logged

Recall

Prompt Answer
Two passes gates first, ear second
What to listen for in an interviewer calm, even, unhurried; no hard onsets
Pace for dense content slightly under natural rate
Why the voice is fixed per session consistency, and an audit trail of what the person heard
Why no cloning here consent and integrity
Draw the shortlist table voice · TTFB · lexicon · by-ear note · decision

The idea

Without it: the voice is picked from a demo page, then fails pronunciation of half the domain terms or sounds wrong for the role.

It does: measures what can be measured, then lets a person judge what can't, on the same lines in each voice.

It costs: a listening session per change, and the discipline not to loosen a gate because a voice sounds nice.

How it works

Voice (14 Oct 2026) Lexicon (gate ≥ 85%) First audio warm p50 (gate ≤ 300 ms) By ear
Flux Sienna 8/8 328–339 ms calm, but hit some words hard
Aura-2 Athena (chosen) 7/8 314 ms calm, smooth, professional: suits an interviewer
Aura-2 Vesta 7/8 319 ms calm but slow; would want a speed setting

Samples of the same lines in each voice and feed: uv run python -m scripts.voice_ab.

Knobs

Knob Default Trade
Speed vendor default slower is clearer for dense questions; Cartesia Sonic 3 allows 0.6–1.5×
Emotion / expressive mode off more human; see persona
Custom or cloned voice off brand voice vs consent

🔊 In our system

What Value Status Why / source
Voice Aura-2 Athena, chosen by ear 14 Oct 2026 goldens Voice change
Gate first-audio gate fails on every voice tried; not loosened goldens
Fixed per session, logged; backup voice switch logged yes design §8.4
Pace slightly under natural rate design §8.4

Measure it

  • Metric — the two gates per voice, plus a by-ear rating on fixed lines.
  • See it — scripts.voice_ab samples side by side.
  • Bounded by — the backup voice.

Pitfalls

Choosing by the vendor's demo

  • Why it's tempting: demos are tuned to sound good.
  • Why it's wrong: your terms and your sentences are not in the demo.
  • Think instead: the same golden lines in every candidate voice.

Connections

… → speak → … — the sound of the agent.

  • voices the persona.
  • gated by TTFB and pronunciation.
  • Say it: Q49

notes.title: Realtime Speech-to-Speech Models — When the Cascade Loses
notes.html:
References

LiveKit — Realtime models (read 16 Oct 2026) · Pipeline shapes

TL;DR

A realtime model hears audio and speaks audio directly. It's faster and more expressive than a cascade and hears tone, but transcripts arrive late, scripted lines aren't guaranteed, and you're tied to one provider. The half-cascade keeps its understanding and swaps in your own TTS for exact control of what is said.

Stage: capture → carry → clean → detect → transcribe → endpoint → think → speak → yield → observe · design time

Flow: audiorealtime modelaudio · half-cascade: audiorealtime modelyour TTSaudio

Recall

Prompt Answer
What realtime models skip separate STT and TTS stages
Transcripts no interims; the user transcript often arrives after the reply
Scripted speech not guaranteed to match the script
Half-cascade in LiveKit modalities=["text"] on the model + a tts on the session
Turn detection LiveKit recommends the model's built-in detector
Draw cascade, realtime and half-cascade as boxes 3 boxes · 1 box · 1 box + TTS

The idea

Without it: a team either rejects realtime models wholesale or adopts them without knowing what they lose.

It does: names the trade and the middle option.

It costs: half-cascade runs two models; full realtime gives up audit and exact wording.

How it works

Provider (LiveKit Inference, 16 Oct 2026) Kind
google/gemini-3.8-live realtime
openai/gpt-live-1 full-duplex
openai/gpt-realtime-2.1 turn-based realtime
xai/grok-voice-3.0 realtime

Also as plugins: Amazon Nova Sonic, Azure OpenAI Realtime, Gemini Live, NVIDIA PersonaPlex, Phonic, Ultravox and others. Limits LiveKit lists: history loads only as text, and OpenAI models may drift toward text-only replies after long histories; add a separate STT if you need live transcripts.

Knobs

Knob Default Trade
modalities audio ["text"] + your TTS: exact words, two models
Turn detection model's own your turn detector needs a separate STT
Separate STT for transcripts off live transcripts, extra cost

🔊 In our system

What Value Status Why / source
Shape cascaded; no realtime model as_built §2
Why exact transcript and word-for-word planned questions are requirements pipeline shapes

Measure it

  • Metric — RealtimeModelMetrics.ttft (first audio token), transcript delay, and scripted-line fidelity against the cascade on the same calls.
  • See it — per-turn metrics; llm_node_ttft and tts_node_ttfb are empty with realtime models.
  • Bounded by — keeping the cascade's interfaces so either can be swapped back.

Pitfalls

Assuming the transcript is free

  • Why it's tempting: the model obviously understood the words.
  • Why it's wrong: user transcripts often arrive after the reply, with no interims; anything that scores or logs text waits.
  • Think instead: add a separate STT if text matters, and price it in.

Connections

… → think → speak → … — the alternative to the whole middle of the pipeline.

  • decided in pipeline shapes.
  • replaces streaming TTS unless half-cascade.
  • Say it: Q10

notes.title: Background Audio and Thinking Sounds
notes.html:
References

LiveKit — Background audio (read 16 Oct 2026)

TL;DR

A separate audio track can play ambience for the whole call and a "thinking" sound (keyboard typing) while the agent works, so a pause reads as activity, not a dropped call.

Stage: capture → carry → clean → detect → transcribe → endpoint → think → speak → yield → observe · per session

The idea

LiveKit (Oct 2026) Detail
BackgroundAudioPlayer publishes a separate track; ambient (loops) and thinking (while the agent thinks) sounds
Built-in clips OFFICE_AMBIENCE, KEYBOARD_TYPING, KEYBOARD_TYPING2
AudioConfig volume (1), probability (1; keep a list's total below 1 to allow silence), fade_in/fade_out (Python)

🔊 In our system

Not used: the design buys responsiveness with latency and honest bridge lines, not sounds (design §8.4). An ambient track would also leak into the candidate's mic, which the echo guard must then handle.

Connections

an alternative to the filler lines in tools and slow work; a persona choice: persona.
